turns.q: guy gets dumped and tells everyone he never even liked her. which one from my notes is that
turns.expect: Rationalization (making excuses that sound logical), from the Defense mechanisms note.
turns.ans: That sounds like rationalization from your Defense mechanisms note: making excuses that sound logical so the hurt feels smaller. Saying he never liked her after being dumped is a classic example. Your note says it's the ego's way of handling painful feelings, which is why it can sound convincing even when it isn't quite true.

turns.expect: No: denial refuses to accept the reality at all; rationalization accepts it but explains it away with a logical-sounding excuse. Notes that denial isn't in their note.
turns.ans:
Good question, and they're close cousins. The difference is whether he accepts what happened.

Denial refuses to accept the fact itself, as if being dumped never happened.
Rationalization accepts the fact but builds a logical-sounding story around it, like "I never even liked her anyway."

Saying he never liked her is mostly rationalization, because he knows she dumped him and is explaining it away. It can slide into denial if he's really refusing to feel the loss. Denial isn't one of the defenses in your note, so it's worth checking your course material for how your instructor defines it.

turns.expect: Uses the psych sense from their Defense mechanisms note (attributing your own unacceptable feelings to someone else), not maps, film projectors or forecasts.
turns.ans:
Projection is a defense mechanism where you attribute your own unacceptable feelings, thoughts or impulses to someone else, so you don't have to face them yourself.

For example, someone who is angry at themselves for being late might insist that everyone else is rushing them or that their friend is always impatient. The feeling is real, but it gets pinned on another person.

It's one of the defense mechanisms the ego uses to manage anxiety from the id's urges and the superego's guilt. In psych nursing, watch for it when a patient blames others for feelings they seem to have themselves.

turns.q: how would i spot it on the unit
turns.expect: Gives a nursing example, e.g. a hostile patient insisting staff are angry at him, and a brief nursing response (stay calm, non-defensive, reflect feelings).
turns.ans:
On the unit, look for a patient who repeatedly blames others for feelings that seem to be their own. Some signs to watch for:

Blaming staff or other patients for their anxiety, anger or distress, such as "Everyone here is trying to get me upset."
Attributing motives to others that don't fit the situation, like assuming a nurse dislikes them when there's no evidence of it.
Saying others are judging, stealing from or plotting against them when they seem to be the one feeling judgmental or resentful.
Reacting to a minor frustration with a strong accusation toward someone nearby.

When you notice it, respond without arguing or confirming the accusation. Reflect the feeling back gently ("It sounds like you're feeling really frustrated right now"), ask open questions about what they're experiencing, and stay calm and consistent. Document the specific words and behaviours you observed, and mention the pattern to your instructor or charge nurse, since it can point to underlying anxiety or other concerns the team should know about.

turns.q: whats the ABC thing in my notes
turns.expect: From the REBT note (Albert Ellis): Activating event, Belief, Consequence.
turns.ans:
The ABC model is part of Rational-Emotive Behavior Therapy (REBT), from Albert Ellis. Your note says:

A, Activating event: the situation or trigger that happens.
B, Belief: how you interpret the event, especially rigid "musts" and "shoulds."
C, Consequence: the emotional and behavioral result that follows from that belief.

The goal of REBT is to dispute the irrational beliefs at B and replace them with rational ones, which changes the consequence at C.

turns.expect: Gives a concrete ABC example, e.g. A: hard practice quiz, B: 'I must get 100% or I'm a failure', C: panic and avoidance; may add disputing the 'must'.
turns.ans:
Here's an ABC example for test anxiety, using the model from your notes:

A (Activating event): You sit down for an exam, read the first question, and your mind goes blank.
B (Belief): "I must know every answer perfectly, and if I blank now, I'll fail the whole course."
C (Consequence): Your heart races, you rush, you stop reading the other questions, and you feel like giving up.

To dispute the belief at B, ask:

Is it actually true that I must get every answer right?
What's the evidence that one blank means I'll fail?
If a friend had this thought, what would I tell them?

A more rational belief: "I'd like to do well, and blanking on one question is uncomfortable, but I can skip it, breathe, and come back to it."

turns.q: after the AV node where does the signal go
turns.expect: From the Cardiac cycle note: bundle of His, then Purkinje fibers.
turns.ans: After the AV node, the impulse travels down the bundle of His (the AV bundle). It then splits into the left and right bundle branches, which carry it down the interventricular septum to the Purkinje fibers. The Purkinje fibers spread through the ventricular walls, so both ventricles contract from the bottom up and push blood out. The AV node's short delay lets the atria finish emptying into the ventricles first.

turns.expect: The SA node, the natural pacemaker.
turns.ans:
The sinoatrial (SA) node starts it. It's a small cluster of specialized cells in the upper wall of the right atrium. Its cells depolarize on their own, without needing a signal from the nerves, which is why it's called the natural pacemaker.

The SA node fires the impulse, which spreads across both atria and makes them contract.
The signal then reaches the AV node, which is the next step you asked about.
At rest the SA node usually fires about 60 to 100 times a minute. The autonomic nervous system and hormones like adrenaline can speed it up or slow it down.

turns.expect: Archduke Franz Ferdinand, June 1914, the spark of WWI per their WWI note (not a band or other person).
turns.ans: Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria-Hungary was shot in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914. His wife, Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg, was killed in the same attack. The shooter was Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb nationalist linked to the group Young Bosnia. The assassination set off the July Crisis, and the alliance system pulled the major powers into World War I.

turns.q: why did that drag everyone in
turns.expect: Explains the alliance chain (Austria-Hungary vs Serbia, Russia backing Serbia, Germany backing Austria, France and Britain joining), tied to Alliances in the MAIN note.
turns.ans:
The assassination set off a chain reaction because of the alliances that had divided Europe into two rival blocs.

Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia for the assassination and sent it an ultimatum on July 23, 1914, that Serbia could not fully accept. Austria-Hungary declared war on July 28.
Germany had promised Austria-Hungary unconditional support, so it backed that stance.
Russia was Serbia's protector and mobilized its army to defend it. Germany, which was allied with Austria-Hungary, saw that as a threat and declared war on Russia on August 1.
France was allied with Russia, so Germany declared war on France on August 3 and invaded Belgium to get around French defenses.
Britain had guaranteed Belgium's neutrality in a 1839 treaty. When Germany invaded Belgium, Britain declared war on Germany on August 4.

Each country was bound to its allies, so a dispute between two small states quickly became a war among the great powers. That's why one assassination in Sarajevo ended up pulling in most of Europe within about a week.

turns.expect: For a nursing student: circulatory shock, inadequate tissue perfusion/oxygen delivery (may mention the everyday sense briefly), not electric shock or a film.
turns.ans:
Shock is a life-threatening condition in which the body's tissues don't get enough blood flow, and so not enough oxygen and nutrients. Without that supply, cells start to fail and organs can be damaged.

The main types are:

Hypovolemic: too little blood or fluid volume, for example from severe bleeding or dehydration.
Cardiogenic: the heart can't pump enough blood, for example after a heart attack.
Distributive: blood vessels widen so much that blood pressure drops. Causes include sepsis, severe allergic reactions (anaphylaxis) and spinal cord injury.
Obstructive: blood flow is blocked, for example by a pulmonary embolism or cardiac tamponade.

Common signs include a fast, weak pulse, low blood pressure, cool or pale or mottled skin, rapid breathing, confusion or restlessness, and low urine output. Shock is a medical emergency that needs urgent treatment.

turns.expect: Hypovolemic, cardiogenic, distributive (septic, anaphylactic, neurogenic) and obstructive.
turns.ans:
The four types of shock are:

Hypovolemic: not enough blood or fluid volume, for example from severe bleeding or dehydration.
Cardiogenic: the heart can't pump enough blood, for example after a heart attack.
Distributive: blood vessels widen so much that blood pressure drops. Causes include sepsis, severe allergic reactions (anaphylaxis) and spinal cord injury.
Obstructive: blood flow is blocked, for example by a pulmonary embolism or cardiac tamponade.

The type tells you the cause, but all four need urgent treatment.

turns.expect: Movement of water across a semipermeable membrane toward the side with more solute.
turns.ans: Osmosis is the movement of water across a semi-permeable membrane from an area of lower solute concentration (more water) to an area of higher solute concentration (less water), until the concentrations on both sides even out. The membrane lets water pass but blocks most dissolved solutes like salts and sugars. It's a passive process, so no energy is needed. In the body it helps cells take in or lose water, and it's why a red blood cell swells in pure water and shrinks in very salty water.

turns.expect: A plainer version, e.g. water moves to where things are saltier/more concentrated to even it out; not a definition of the word 'simple'.
turns.ans: Sure. Osmosis is water moving across a membrane, from where there's more water to where there's less, so the two sides even out. Think of it like this: water sneaks through the membrane to dilute the saltier or sugary side. No energy needed, it just flows on its own.

turns.expect: e.g. raisins swelling in water, or red blood cells swelling in a hypotonic IV fluid and shrinking in a hypertonic one.
turns.ans: Here's an example: a red blood cell placed in pure water takes in water by osmosis, because the water outside is more dilute, so the cell swells and can burst. Put the same cell in a very salty solution and water flows out of it, so it shrinks and wrinkles. In both cases the water moves to even out the concentration on each side of the membrane.
